I'm a historic costumer. I've got seven of these. I know what I'm talking about. Corsets are not necessarily uncomfortable. My tightest one gives me a three inch waist compression and I can wear it all day without a problem. I prefer my mid-Victorian work corset to a bra. They actually aren't the most inconvenient thing about historic styles; the sleeves of 1840s styles or the bodices on Natural Form dresses are so much worse. The really bad style elements had less to do with muh patriarchy than it did overall cultural trends as determined by queens, duchesses, and other rich ladies. I'm not saying that no woman ever forced herself into a ridiculously painful corset in order to wear this or that dress to some event, but that wasn't daily life.

In reality, corsets provided a stable body shape to support the fashionable silhouette of the period, while addressing the boob problem. You have to remember, this was before stretch fabrics had been invented, so clothes had to be fitted very carefully to an individual's body. Patterning was an art we developed over the course of about five hundred years, so dealing with the curves of the human body was difficult. Corsets made it easier.

For a couple hundred years, with the triangular styles of the 1600s-1700s, the point wasn't even waist reduction but general shaping (and in some instances, bust compression). In the early 1800s, corsets shrunk to the point of almost disappearing completely, and then came back in the 1830s, with waist shaping as an additional feature. The waist compression was taken to extremes only in the 1870s-90s by a small number of fashionable ladies. This trend was so hated by women that a female doctor invented an entirely new style of corset in an attempt to address the problem, which was of course then turned into a ridiculously silly style itself.

The lacing thing is completely untrue. "Fifty laces" doesn't mean anything in reality... are they talking about the number of eyelets? All corset styles have ONE lacing ribbon that runs smoothly from top to bottom. Men would only have been expected to unlace a corset completely in the Tudor to Georgian periods; split metal busks in the 1800s made this unnecessary. I don't know about the marriage ceremony thing, but it does not pass the smell test in any way.

Children did wear corsets, but this was because it was thought to be necessary for proper posture and growth. Children of both sexes wore them, and of course, girls transitioned into adult corsets as they went into puberty.

Again, not making excuses, but whoever made this meme is an ignorant idiot.
